gallery.caption: Taped on carefully, with a name written underneath.
gallery.title: Two paper wings on an old bicycle

objectives: Follow a bicycle flight from the courtyard to the roof garden and back.
Name the three parts of the flying bicycle adventure.
Use five new words about flying in your own sentences.
Say why the bicycle needed another rider.
Retell the adventure to someone else in the right order.
Tell a friend the small lesson at the end.

sections.body:
This is a story about Nam. He is eleven years old and he rides an old bicycle every day.

The bicycle is his grandfather's. It is heavy and rusty and the bell only makes a small tired sound. Nam loves it anyway.

One afternoon, under the stairs in the courtyard, he finds it again. And this time there are two **wings** on it. They are made of old newspaper and tape, and they are shaped like bird wings.

A good adventure has a shape. It has a beginning, a middle and an end. The beginning tells you who is going and why. The middle brings the surprise. The end gives you something worth keeping.

This flight has that shape. At the beginning, Nam rings the bell three times and the bicycle lifts off the ground. In the middle, the wind over the old quarter is stronger than he expected. At the end, he learns something about the bicycle that nobody told him.

Read it slowly. Then tell it to someone else. That is how an adventure becomes yours.
examples: This story is about a boy whose bicycle can fly.
A good adventure has a beginning, a middle and an end.
I can tell this story again tomorrow.
sections.heading: What this flying bicycle is about

sections.body:
Nam pushes the bicycle across the courtyard. The **pedals** are stiff. He pushes them once, twice, three times, and the bell ring comes out of nowhere: ding, ding, ding.

The wings move.

Not much at first. The newspaper lifts a little, like a flag in the wind. Nam stops pedalling. The wings drop.

He pedals again. Ding, ding, ding. This time the front wheel lifts off the ground. It is only a finger's width up. Nam's heart jumps into his throat.

He pedals faster. The bicycle rises up the wall like a slow escalator. Nam finds himself sitting on the wall. Then he is on the roof of the noodle shop, with his feet dangling over the street.

Below him the old quarter is waking up. Someone waters the potted mint. A cat walks along a wall. The smell of coffee and fried dough floats up to the roof.

Nam laughs. The sound is a bit frightening, so he stops laughing and pedals instead.

Then he rings the bell one more time. The bicycle flies out over the lake. The whole city opens below him like a map he has never seen.
examples: Ding, ding, ding, and the wings lifted.
He pedals faster and the bicycle climbs the wall.
The city below him looked like a map he had never seen.
sections.heading: How the flight began

sections.body:
Flying is easy for about one minute.

Then the **wind** over the rooftops finds him. The wind is warm. It comes fast off the lake. It pushes the bicycle sideways, towards the tall building with the big clock.

Nam is not a brave boy. He is a boy who likes his grandmother's phở and hates being laughed at. Right now he is very high and very far from the ground.

He pedals harder. It does not help. The wings flap, but the wind is stronger than paper.

Then the bicycle begins to sink. Not crash. Just sink, slowly, the way a paper boat sinks in a bowl. Down towards the water.

Nam is not alone. On the road below, a girl on a pink bicycle has been looking up at him for a while. That is Mai. She pedals hard, catches up with him at the last rooftop, and grabs the back of his saddle.

The bicycle stops sinking.

The wings lift again. Nam understands it at once: it does not fly because of the wings, and not because of the bell. It flies because somebody on the ground is holding on. The wings hold the bicycle up only while two people share it.
examples: The warm wind pushed the bicycle sideways.
The bicycle sank slowly, the way a paper boat sinks.
It flies only while two people share it.
sections.heading: The middle: the wind over the rooftops

sections.body:
They land on the roof garden of an old house near the lake. Nam has never known this place existed.

There are pots of mint and holy basil. There is a water tank, and a bench with a cat asleep on it. Nam's grandmother's brother used to work here, when the house was still a workshop. She used to bring him lunch.

They eat two buns from a paper bag. Mai tells him the bicycle was her grandfather's too. It sat in her family's garage for thirty years. Nobody knew it could fly.

Then comes the hard part. The way down.

Nam tries to fly down alone. The wings lift one side and then the other. The bicycle turns in a slow circle above the roofs. Down is much harder than up.

"Ring the bell," Mai says from the stairwell. "I will hold the saddle and walk down the stairs."

So they do that. Ding, ding, ding. The bicycle goes down slowly, side by side with the stairwell window, while Mai walks and holds on. Down four floors. Down five. Down to the courtyard, where Nam's grandmother is waiting with her arms folded.

She looks at the paper wings. She looks at the bicycle. Then she looks at Nam.

"Your grandfather," she says, "could never ride it alone either."
examples: There were pots of mint and a cat asleep on the bench.
Down was much harder than up.
Your grandfather could never ride it alone either.
sections.heading: The surprise: the roof garden and the long way down

sections.body:
These are the words you will meet in this story. Learn them here, and you can use them in your own sentences.

A **bicycle** is a machine with two wheels that you push with your feet. A good bicycle makes your legs feel like they have a strong friend.

A **pedal** is the flat part of a bicycle that your foot stands on. When you push the pedals, the wheels turn.

A **wing** is the flat part that helps a bird to lift into the air. On this bicycle, the wings are only paper, but they still lift.

A **bell** is the small metal thing on a bicycle that makes a sound when you press it. Nam's bell is old and a bit tired.

A **rooftop** is the flat top of a building. In the old quarter, the rooftops are close enough to almost touch.
examples: You push the pedals and the wheels turn.
The bell rings when you press it.
Two rooftops in the old quarter are almost touching.

sections.body:
What did Nam learn? He learned that magic in this story is not in the paper wings. It is in the rule nobody wrote down: the bicycle flies only while somebody on the ground is holding on.

He also learned that going down is harder than going up. The way down is always walked with someone.

Here is how to tell this adventure to someone. Keep the order, and the surprise will land in the right place.

Start with the bicycle in the courtyard and the three rings of the bell. Tell the wind and the sinking in the middle, and the girl who grabbed the saddle. Save the long way down for last. Then say the small lesson in one short sentence.

The lesson of this adventure is this: nobody flies very far alone.
examples: The story starts with three rings of the bell.
The surprise comes at the very end.
sections.heading: The small lesson, and how to tell the story
steps: Start with the character: Nam and the old bicycle in the courtyard.
Tell the middle: three rings, the rooftops, the wind and the sinking.
Tell the surprise: Mai on the pink bicycle, and the rule of the saddle.
End with the lesson: nobody flies very far alone.

item.summary: Nam finds his grandfather's old bicycle with two paper wings taped to the frame, and it flies over the rooftops of the old quarter. Follow him past the lake, the wind and the moment he thinks he is lost. After reading, you can retell the flight, use five new words about flying in your own sentences, and say why the bicycle needed a second pair of hands.
item.title: The Flying Bicycle Adventure
